## LEARNING OBJECTIVES

<br>By the end of this lecture you should be able to:

- Explain how cellular heterogeneity impacts measurements of drug responses.
- Explain how tissue spatial organization impacts measurements of drug responses.
- Use cell-specific molecular signatures to evaluate and screen pharmacological responses.
- Compare cell-specific dose-response relationships to tissue-level measurements for evaluating drug efficacy and safety.

<!-- ======================================================================

     ====================================================================== -->

## LOSING HETEROGENEITY IN THE AVERAGES

<br>In the last lecture we examined signatures measured from a **whole piece of tissue** or measured in <i>bulk</i>. That number is an average over every cell and every location in the sample.

- Different cell types respond to the same drug in different ways.
- Cells sit in organized neighborhoods, and location changes their exposure and behavior.
- An average can hide a strong response in a small group of cells.

## TISSUES ARE MIXTURES OF CELL TYPES {#l2-heterogeneity}

<br>A bulk RNA-seq measurement is a **weighted average** of every cell in the sample, weighted by how many cells of each type there are and how much RNA each makes.

- A liver sample contains hepatocytes, but also immune, endothelial, and stellate cells.
- A change in the average does not tell you which cell type changed.

<!-- PLACEHOLDER: figure — pie of cell types beside the bulk expression bar it produces -->
::: placeholder-box
PLACEHOLDER — figure: cell-type proportions feeding one bulk expression value
:::

## SAME BULK CHANGE, DIFFERENT STORIES

<br>Two very different things can produce the same change in a bulk signature:

- **Composition**: the drug changed *how many* cells of a type are present (for example, immune cells moved into the tissue)
- **State**: the drug changed *what each cell does*, with the same number of cells

<!-- PLACEHOLDER: figure — two tissues with the same bulk readout but different cell-level causes -->
::: placeholder-box
PLACEHOLDER — figure: same bulk readout, composition change versus state change
:::

<br>Emerging technologies such as single-cell and single-nucleus RNA-seq measure expression separately in thousands of individual cells.

::: notes
A toy liver of 10 cells by 10 genes; bulk is the average of the cells. Step 1 (no lock-in): slide the number of immune cells and watch the bulk row. Immune genes rise and hepatocyte genes dilute. Step 2: keep 2 immune cells in 10 and turn up the immune genes inside each immune cell; only the immune genes move. Step 3: Story A (more immune cells) and Story B (same cells, matching increase in immune gene expression) give the same bulk signal for the immune genes, so bulk alone cannot tell composition from state. The only clue is the small dilution of the hepatocyte genes in Story A, which is lost in real-world variability. This is the first activity, so allow about 10 minutes.
:::

## LOCATION CHANGES THE RESPONSE {#l2-spatial}

<br>Cells in a tissue are arranged in organized neighborhoods, and cells of the same type can behave differently depending on where they are.

- In the liver, cells near the central vein and cells near the portal vein express different sets of genes, including drug-metabolizing enzymes
- Acetaminophen injury concentrates around the central vein, where those enzymes are highest

<!-- PLACEHOLDER: figure — liver lobule showing zonation and the region of injury -->
::: placeholder-box
PLACEHOLDER — figure: liver lobule with the zones of enzyme expression and the zone of injury
:::

## MEASURING EXPRESSION IN SPACE

<br>Spatial transcriptomics keeps track of where each measurement came from.

- **Spot-based** methods capture a small area that can hold several cells, so a spot is a small mixture
- **Imaging-based** methods read out genes at the level of single cells or molecules, often with a targeted gene panel
- Resolution, number of genes, and cost trade off against each other

<!-- PLACEHOLDER: figure — spot grid over a tissue versus single-cell resolution overlay -->
::: placeholder-box

:::

## SCREENING WITH CELL-SPECIFIC SIGNATURES

<br>The signature matching from bulk approaches still applies:

- Compare a compound's response in the cell type of interest with known drugs.
- Look for the effect in the intended cell type and for off-target effects in the others.
- A tissue-level match can miss a response that only one cell type shows.

::: notes
This repeats the inverse-signature idea from lecture 1, now with single-cell data. In an inflammatory liver disease, immune cells and hepatocytes change very differently. Two candidate drugs are shown: one is the mirror image of the hepatocyte signature, the other of the immune-cell signature. The question states that the immune cells drive the disease, so the task is to find the drug that is the mirror image of the immune-cell column. After the check, the feedback depends on the answer. If students pick the hepatocyte drug, say that it is a sensible choice if you only had bulk data: the bulk column (hepatocytes ~85% of cells) looks like the hepatocyte signature, so a bulk screen ranks that drug first, but the disease is driven by the immune cells. If they pick the immune drug, they get the same bulk caveat as the take-away. Which letter is correct changes with the seed.
:::

## TISSUE-LEVEL DOSE-RESPONSE CAN MISLEAD {#l2-dose-response}

<br>If only a fraction of the cells respond, the tissue-level curve shows only a fraction of that response.

- A strong response in a small group of cells looks weak in the average.
- The apparent threshold shifts to higher doses, or the response drops below detection altogether.
- A rare, sensitive cell type can be the real target of toxicity.

<!-- PLACEHOLDER: figure — a sharp cell-type curve next to the flatter diluted tissue curve -->
::: placeholder-box
PLACEHOLDER — figure: a cell-type dose-response curve beside the diluted bulk curve
:::

## CELL- AND SPATIAL- DOSE RESPONSE MODELING

<br>This is an actively evolving field and what was discussed is largely theoretical. Single-cell and spatial data poses unique challenges for dose-response modeling.

- The data is very sparse leading to a lot of zeroes presenting some statistical challenges.
- There is limited data to develop and test these methods. Single-cell methods are now more affordable (~10X bulk approaches) but spatial methods are note highly scalable today (~100 - 1000X bulk approaches). 

<!-- PLACEHOLDER: figure — benchmark dose for each cell type versus the tissue-level value -->
::: placeholder-box

</iframe>

::: notes
Start with the bulk dose-response curve for Gene X and the dashed line at 10% response: one curve, one dose. Tick "Split into cell types" to reveal the four sigmoidal curves it is built from. The same 10% line now crosses at several doses: one cell type is far more sensitive than the bulk value suggests (a small population hidden by the average), and one barely responds in this dose range. The dose slider shows each curve's response at a chosen dose; at the bulk 10% dose, the most sensitive cell type is already well above 10%. A new seed changes which cell types are sensitive.
:::

## PUTTING IT TOGETHER

<br>Four objectives, four activities:

- **LO 1** — A tissue measurement averages over cell types, so composition and state changes can look alike.
- **LO 2** — Location shapes the response, and capture area decides what you can see.
- **LO 3** — Cell-specific signatures let you screen for the effect you want, in the cells you want.
- **LO 4** — Cell-specific dose-response can reveal sensitivity that the tissue average hides.
